families.name: Bantu
families.description: Largest language family in Kenya (~65% of population). Spread across central, western, and coastal regions.

families.name: Nilotic
families.description: Second largest family (~30%). Includes Plains Nilotes (Maasai, Turkana, Samburu, Teso), Highland Nilotes (Kalenjin, Pokot), and River-Lake Nilotes (Luo).

families.name: Cushitic
families.description: Found in northern and eastern Kenya (~3%). Includes Somali, Borana/Oromo, Rendille, and Daasanach (Dhaasanac).

families.name: Other
families.description: Includes Swahili (Bantu-based national & official lingua franca), English (official), and minor language isolates.

languages.name: Kikuyu (Gĩkũyũ)
languages.notes: Largest mother-tongue community in the central highlands (Kiambu/Kabeti, Murang'a/Metumi/Fort Hall, and Nyeri/Gaki around Mount Kenya [Kĩrĩnyaga / Kĩlinya-tha / Kĩreĩra / Donyo Egere]); documented in Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894 'Discovery of Lakes Rudolf and Stefanie', Vol. I, Chs. V–VI, pp. 220–221, 234–236, 286–309 [361], 362–366, 371–375 — audited 100% line-by-line across the Aug. 23, 1887 Ngongo Bagas blood-brotherhood with Miani, Karanja & Waiyaki, all 68 parallel ravines from Nairobi to Thegu incl. the Chania liana suspension bridge, 600-ft. Maragua gorge & 700-ft. Mathioya chasm, Subugo forest fortifications, kihingo gates & ngurunga pitfalls with muriju [Acokanthera Schimperi] poison, 'U-u-u-ui! Ngai!' & 'Mirema!', Muthamaki/Athuri & Anake, mburi ya thayu & kuhoria tatha chanting 'Thayu! Thayu!', Aturi smiths, ruhiu, kahiu, kiondo, mwatũ, njohi/uhi, njingiri, corno & 7–8 ft. muro digging-sticks, 3-tier ridge crop zoning, chiefs Kihara, Gathirimu, Getura, Karanja wa Maragua, Wamugunda of Tetu, Sept. 16 Mathira 7-step githathi peace covenant over a white ram & black goat, Chief Kihura at Ndoro, and the Oct. 8–14, 1887 first ascent of Mount Kenia across 5 vertical zones to 15,355 ft. [4,680 m] with Lobelia Telekii Schweinfurth), Rev. Fr. A. Hémery, C.S.Sp. (1903 'English-Kikuyu Hand-Book'), Hildegarde Hinde (1904 'Vocabularies of the Kamba and Kikuyu Languages of East Africa'), Rev. A. W. McGregor (1904 'English-Kikuyu Vocabulary: Compiled for the Use of the C.M.S. Missions in East Africa', SPCK London, printed by Richard Clay & Sons, Limited, London and Bungay, Fort Smith / Kabeti 1901–1902, Preface dated London, May 1903, pp. [i]–iv, 5–192 [PDF pp. 1–201, Stanford University Libraries Copy PL 8379.4 .M3 C.1, Dr. & Mrs. Robert A. Rennie bookplate] — audited 100% line-by-line across all 7,094 Markdown lines), W. Scoresby & Katherine Routledge (1910 'With a Prehistoric People: The Akikúyu of British East Africa'), Hobley (1910, 1922), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), BFBS (1921), and Martha Michieka & Leonard Muaka (2016, Ch. 28 'Humor in Kenyan comedy', pp. 559–576, Ex. 2–3, 8, 10, 14).

languages.name: Dholuo (Luo)
languages.notes: River-Lake Nilotes of the Lake Victoria basin; documented in Rev. Charles New (1873), Rev. Thomas Wakefield & Robert Needham Cust (1883 'A Sketch of the Modern Languages of Africa', Vol. I, Ch. XI.D 'Nile Sub-Group', pp. 273–287: XXI. Kavirondo on Victoria Nyanza pp. 284–285, Wakefield's MS Kavirondo Vocabulary from a Swahíli caravan traveller, and first comparative proof of marked affinity with I. Shilluk/Dyur [Luoh/Lwo, Bellanda & Dembo] pp. 275–276, XVIII. Lúr [Luoh] pp. 282–283 & XX. Shúli [Gani/Shefalu] pp. 283–284), Hobley (1902, 1903), Johnston (1902), Northcote (1907), Roscoe/Willis (1915), Mill-Hill Fathers (1920), BFBS (1921), and Martha Michieka & Leonard Muaka (2016, Ch. 28 'Humor in Kenyan comedy', pp. 559–576, Ex. 2–3, 10, 13, 15–16: academic title prefixes & Sheng sibilant substitution 'shrubbing' sida, shitikashel, aishishi).

languages.name: Kalenjin
languages.notes: Highland Nilotes (Nandi, Kipsigis/Lumbwa [Il Kakesan], Tugen/Kamasia [Kapteberewa & Nderois], Marakwet & Endo/Ndo [Chebleng], Keiyo/Elgeyo, Cherang'any, Kabkamat/Olmo, Sangwirr, Uasin Gishu Moiven/Muttia/Il-Mokwan/I-Sirikwa, Sabaot, Pökoot); documented in Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894, Vol. I, Ch. VI, pp. 383–384: Kamasia hills [5,500–7,000 ft.] and Kerio valley grain trade with the Elgeyo and Marakwet yielding 65 loads of mtama and wimbi in Nov.–Dec. 1887), Hobley (1902, 1903, 1910), Johnston (1902), A. C. Hollis (1909 'The Nandi: Their Language and Folk-Lore'), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Beech (1911), BFBS (1921), Rottland (1982), Creider & Creider (1983, 1989), Toweett (1979), Mietzner (2016), Jerono (2018), Sitienei Jepkoech (2018), Michael Diercks & Meghana Rao (2019 'Upward-oriented complementizer agreement with subjects and objects in Kipsigis', in Clem, Jenks & Sande, eds., 'Theory and description in African linguistics', Berlin: Language Science Press, Ch. 20, pp. 369–393, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.3367166 — audited 100% line-by-line across Subj-CA ɑ-lɛ/i-lɛ/kɔ-lɛ/kɛ-lɛ/o-lɛ, Obj-CA -lɛ-ndʒ-ɑn/-in/-i/-ɛtʃ/-ɔɔɣ, verum focus & overt C-raising), Meredith Landman (2019 'Nominal quantification in Kipsigis', Ch. 25, pp. 481–498, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.3367177 — audited 100% line-by-line across tugul vs. age tugul), Kouneli (2021), and Joost Zwarts, Andrew Chelimo & Prisca Jerono (2023; 2024 'The reflexive in Kalenjin: Its syntactic status and semantic functions', Language Science Press, Ch. 21, pp. 539–556, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.11210482).

languages.name: Luhya (Luyia)
languages.notes: 17+ Western Bantu dialects including Wanga (Luhanga of Buhanga), Bukusu/Masaba (Lubukusu), Kabras, Nyala, Marama, Tsotso, Tiriki, Idakho (Lwitaxo), Isukha, and Maragoli (Logoori / Luragooli [rag] JE41); documented in Hobley (1902, 1903), Johnston (1902, 1919), Rev. J. B. Purvis (1907; 1909 'Through Uganda to Mount Elgon', Ch. XV 'The Language of the Bagisu [Lumasaba]', pp. 317–332 & Ch. XVI 'Folklore', pp. 333–351 — audited 100% line-by-line across 6 double-prefix classes, Bimanyisa Kusoma & Katabo Kanyoherwako, Nayu's July 20, 1907 letter, Lord's Prayer, 3 hymns, 17 'Why?' idioms, greetings & 3 Bagisu fables), Roscoe (1915), Rev. N. Stam (1929 'The Bahanga', Catholic Anthropological Conference Vol. I, No. 4, pp. 143–179 — audited 100% line-by-line), Doris L. Payne, Sara Pacchiarotti & Mokaya Bosire, eds. (2016 'Diversity in African languages', Berlin: Language Science Press, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.281 — audited 100% line-by-line across Chs. 9, 11, 12, 15, 25 & 28), and Naga Selvanathan (2019 'A case based account of Bantu IAV-focus', in Clem, Jenks & Sande, eds., 'Theory and description in African linguistics', Ch. 32, pp. 623–645, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.3367191, Lubukusu consultant Justine Sikuku — audited 100% line-by-line).

languages.name: Kamba (Kĩkamba)
languages.notes: Central Bantu language of Eastern Kenya across 4 regional divisions (Ulu/Yulu [kīkamba kīluŋgalu & Kīluŋgu], East Ukamba/Kitui [aþaisu / kīþaisu], Kīkumbuliu & Mumonī, plus Anoka on Mt. Noka and the 1836 Rabai diaspora); documented in Krapf (1850), Last (1885), Hinde (1904), Hobley (1910, 1922), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), Gerhard Lindblom (1920 'The Akamba in British East Africa: An Ethnological Monograph', 2nd Ed., Enlarged, Archives d'Études Orientales Vol. 17, Uppsala, pp. I–XII, 1–607, Figs. 1–167 — audited 100% line-by-line), BFBS (1921), Michieka & Muaka (2016, Ch. 28, p. 569, Ex. 12), and Patrick Jones & Jake Freyer (2019 'Reconsidering tone and melodies in Kikamba', in Clem, Jenks & Sande, eds., 'Theory and description in African linguistics', Berlin: Language Science Press, Ch. 10, pp. 177–198, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.3367138 — audited 100% line-by-line across Tables 1–7, Ex. 1–16 & Fig. 1).

languages.name: Somali
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic language of North Eastern Kenya; documented in Krapf & Isenberg (1840, pp. iv–v, xi, xiii), Rigby (1850, 1866), Burton (1856), Hunter (1880), Robert Needham Cust (1883, Vol. I, Ch. IX.C.I 'Somáli', pp. 119, 121), Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894 'Discovery of Lakes Rudolf and Stefanie', Vol. I, pp. 10–12, 33, 123–124, 162, 174), de Larajasse (1897), Lt. J. W. C. Kirk (1903 'Notes on the Somali Language', OUP, pp. i–xii, 1–83 — audited 100% line-by-line; and 1905 'A Grammar of the Somali Language'), BFBS (1921), Morgan Nilsson (2016 'Somali gender polarity revisited', Ch. 23, pp. 451–466, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.494), Christopher R. Green & Evan Jones (2019 'Notes on the morphology of Marka [Af-Ashraaf]', Ch. 7, pp. 119–134, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.3367132), Wendell Kimper, Wm. G. Bennett, Christopher R. Green & Kristine Yu (2019 'Acoustic correlates of harmony classes in Somali', Ch. 11, pp. 199–212, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.3367140), and Derek Nurse (2019 'When Northern Swahili met southern Somali', Ch. 33, pp. 649–665, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.3367193).

languages.name: Kisii (Ekegusii)
languages.notes: Eastern Lake Victoria Bantu language of the Kisii Highlands; documented in Hobley (1902) and Johnston (1902, 1919).

languages.name: Meru (Kĩmĩĩrũ)
languages.notes: Mount Kenya & Tana valley Bantu cluster (Imenti, Tigania, Igembe, Mwimbi, Chuka, and Kĩtharaka); documented in Hobley (1910), Arthur M. Champion (1912 'The Atharaka', JRAI Vol. 42, pp. 68–90 + Plate X — audited 100% line-by-line across 5 male & 6 female age-grades, Mutialu smithy kianda, 4 dances, Thela Luku 5th-night death rite, blood-money, Chiama & 14 clans), Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), Prof. Kithaka wa Mberia (2004 'The Phonology of Borrowed Words in Kitharaka', Occasional Papers in Language and Linguistics Vol. 2, pp. 45–57, Examples 1–18 — audited 100% line-by-line across 7 vowels, 14 consonants, /p,b,f,v/ → /β/, /s,z/ → /s/ or /ð/, productive Dahl's Law /k/ → /ɣ/ in moɣatɛ & karaɣita, n-propping of /d/ in ndawa & nderesa, and prefix reanalysis duka → ruka → nduka), and Martha Michieka & Leonard Muaka (2016, Ch. 28 'Humor in Kenyan comedy', p. 562, Ex. 1).

languages.name: Maasai (Maa)
languages.notes: Plains Nilotes (Eastern Nilotic, across 4 Clans ['L-Aiser, Il-Meñgana, Il-Mokesen, Il-Molelyan], 2 Moieties ['L-oodo-kishu & 'L-oorook-kishu], 19 Sub-Families [Il-gilat], and 5 Districts [Il-Kaputiei, En-aiposha, 'L-Oitai, Il-Kisonko, 'L-Uasinkishu], plus Laikipiak, Segellai, and Tigirri); documented in Krapf (1854 'Vocabulary of the Engútuk Eloikób'), Erhardt & Krapf (1857 'Vocabulary of the Enguduk Iloigob'), Farler & Wakefield (1882), Robert Needham Cust (1883, Vol. I, Ch. X.A.V–VI, pp. 149–152), Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894 'Discovery of Lakes Rudolf and Stefanie', Vol. I, Chs. I–IV & VI, pp. 12–14, 84, 100, 131, 206–236 [285], 367–385 — audited 100% line-by-line), Hildegarde Hinde (1901), Johnston (1902), A. C. Hollis & Sir Charles Eliot (1905), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Hobley (1910), W. S. & K. Routledge (1910), BFBS (1921), Tucker & Mpaayei (1955), and Jonathan Moodie (2016 'Number marking in Lopit, an Eastern Nilotic language', in 'Diversity in African languages', Berlin: Language Science Press, Ch. 21, pp. 397–416, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.492: Eastern Nilotic tripartite number marking and Maasai Greater Plural eng-ker 'sheep' → ing-kerr-a 'sheep [pl.]' → ing-kerr-ai 'herds of sheep' in Table 18, p. 412).

languages.name: Turkana (Ng'aturukana)
languages.notes: Plains Nilotes (Ateker branch: 16 principal tribes and 19 Ngoitunya & Ngolio attegir clans); documented in Höhnel (1894), Johnston (1902), Purvis (1909), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Beech (1911), Barton (1921), Dimmendaal (1983, 2000), and Jonathan Moodie (2016, Ch. 21, pp. 397–416, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.492).

languages.name: Embu (Kĩembu)
languages.notes: Mount Kenya southeastern slopes (Embu & Mbeere); documented in Dundas (1915), Johnston (1919), and Hobley (1922).

languages.name: Taita (Kidawida)
languages.notes: Taita Hills Bantu (Dawida, Sagala, Kasigau); documented in Shaw (1885), Taylor (1891), Wray (1894), Werner (1915), Johnston (1919), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Swahili (Kiswahili)
languages.notes: National & official language of Kenya (including Kiamu, Kimvita, Kitikuu/Bajuni, Kipate, Kingozi, Ki-Jezirati/Ki-Jizirat of Pemba, and Kiunguja); documented in Krapf (1850, 1882), Bishop Edward Steere (1870 'Swahili Tales, as Told by Natives of Zanzibar'; 1918 'Swahili Exercises'), Farler & Wakefield (1882), Robert Needham Cust (1883, Vol. I), Bishop Edward Steere & A. C. Madan (1894 'A Handbook of the Swahili Language, as Spoken at Zanzibar', 4th Ed.), Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894 'Discovery of Lakes Rudolf and Stefanie', Vol. I, Chs. I–III, pp. [v]–xx, 1–205 — audited 100% line-by-line), Taylor (1891), George W. Bateman (1901 'Zanzibar Tales'), A. C. Madan (1903 'Swahili-English Dictionary'), Mrs. F. Burt & Rev. W. E. Taylor (1910 'Swahili Grammar and Vocabulary'), Stigand (1915), Mervyn W. H. Beech (1918 'Aids to the Study of Ki-Swahili: Four Studies Compiled and Annotated'), Alice Werner (1918 'Swahili Poetry', BSOS Vol. 1, Pt. 2, pp. 113–127; 1919, 1933), Deo Ngonyani & Nancy Jumwa Ngowa (2016, Ch. 14, pp. 255–271, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.485), Martha Michieka & Leonard Muaka (2016, Ch. 28, pp. 559–576, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.499), Isaac Gould & Tessa Scott (2019 'An experimental investigation of scope and reconstruction in Swahili relative clauses', Ch. 23, pp. 441–462, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.3367173), Jonathan Pesetsky (2019 'Semantic gender in Swahili', Ch. 29, pp. 555–570, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.3367185), Derek Nurse (2019 'When Northern Swahili met southern Somali', Ch. 33, pp. 649–665, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.3367193), Mohamed Mwamzandi (2022, Ch. 13, pp. 227–246), and John Goldsmith & Fidèle Mpiranya (2022).

languages.name: Mijikenda
languages.notes: Nine coastal Sabaki sub-groups (Giriama, Digo [Chidigo, [dig] E73], Duruma, Chonyi, Jibana, Kambe, Ribe, Rabai, Kauma); documented in Krapf (1850), Krapf & Rebmann (1887), Taylor (1891), Werner (1915), Johnston (1919), BFBS (1921), and Steve Nicolle (2016 'Variation in the expression of information structure in eastern Bantu languages', in Doris L. Payne, Sara Pacchiarotti & Mokaya Bosire, eds., 'Diversity in African languages', Berlin: Language Science Press, Ch. 20, pp. 377–395, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.491 — audited 100% line-by-line across Table 1 [864 Digo clauses from Kwale District, Kenya] & Ex. 1–30 on left/right topic dislocation, obligatory clefts for subject argument focus, and VS thetic sentences).

languages.name: Borana (Oromo)
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic language (Borana [including the Royal Clan Karayu of Chief Gedu in Ethiopia], Gabbra, Sakuye, Wata, and Tana River Orma — Barareta Oromo [descended from Ana Bake], Kofira Oromo [from Ana Dima/Ana Bake], and Migo Oromo [from Ana Kare]); documented in Rev. J. L. Krapf & Rev. C. W. Isenberg (1840 'An Imperfect Outline of the Elements of the Galla Language', London: CMS / L. & G. Seeley / Richard Watts, pp. [i]–xiv, [1]–16 [Bodleian Library copy] — audited 100% line-by-line; plus 1842 & 1850), Tutschek (1844–1845), Robert Needham Cust (1883 'A Sketch of the Modern Languages of Africa', Vol. I, Ch. IX.C.II 'Galla or Orómo', pp. 122–125 — audited 100% line-by-line), Foot (1913), Werner (1915), BFBS (1921), Mikael Samson & R. G. Darroch (1944, pp. 370–394), and Griefenow-Mewis (1996).

languages.name: Rendille
languages.notes: Omo-Tana East Cushitic camel-herding pastoralists of the Kaisut and Chalbi plains (including the historical Naroshon section on the Sogota–Lomello plains); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Höhnel (1894), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Hobley (1910), Fleming (1964), Heine (1976, 1978), Pillinger & Galboran (1999), and Blažek (2011).

languages.name: Teso (Ateso)
languages.notes: Eastern Nilotic (Ateker) language spoken in Busia County and eastern Uganda; documented in Hobley (1902), Johnston (1902), Purvis (1909), Kitching (1915), Roscoe (1915), BFBS (1921), Hilders & Lawrance (1956), and Jonathan Moodie (2016 'Number marking in Lopit, an Eastern Nilotic language', in 'Diversity in African languages', Berlin: Language Science Press, Ch. 21, pp. 397–416, DOI: 10.17169/langsci.b121.492: Teso tripartite Singular / Plural / Greater Plural paradigm e-tunga-nan 'person' → i-tunga 'people' → i-tunga-sinei 'mankind' in Table 18, p. 412).

languages.name: Pokomo
languages.notes: Tana River (Galana Maro) Sabaki Bantu language across Malachini and Upper Pokomo; documented in Krapf (1850), Würtz (1895, 1896), Werner (1913, 1915, 1933), Johnston (1919–1922 #13 Pωkωmω), BFBS (1921), and Mikael Samson & R. G. Darroch (1944, pp. 370–394 & Full-Page Sketch Map — audited 100% line-by-line).

languages.name: Samburu
languages.notes: Northern Maa (Plains Nilotic) pastoralists (including historical Il Doigio, Lorogishu / Kwakituk on Angata e-'m-barta, Lobbeyok, and Il Leikipiak sections on the Leikipia plateau); documented in Krapf (1854), Farler & Wakefield (1882), Cust (1883, Vol. I, pp. 149–152), Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894, Vol. I, Ch. VI, pp. 367–385: traverse of the 8 Mount Kenia glacier streams, upper Guaso Nyiro, Leikipia plateau [6,000–6,850 ft.] with abandoned kraals of the Il Leikipiak routed ~20 yrs. earlier, Marmanet swamp, Ongalea mountains [172-lb elephant tusks] & Larabwal to Njemps), Johnston (1902), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), and Hobley (1910).

languages.name: Ilchamus (Njemps)
languages.notes: Lake Baringo Maa-speaking irrigation farmers and fishermen (Njamus / Nyarusi across Njemps Kubwa [Liabori], Njemps Ndogo [Lekepir], and Korvan, comprising 16 clans from 6 tribes); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Cust (1883, Vol. I, pp. 149–152), Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894 'Discovery of Lakes Rudolf and Stefanie', Vol. I, Ch. VI, pp. 367–385 [417–435] & 4 Fold-out Maps — audited 100% line-by-line), Johnston (1902), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), and Beech (1911).

languages.name: Pokot (Pökoot)
languages.notes: Highland Nilotes (Northern Kalenjin branch, historically Suk / Bawgott across 11 geographical divisions and 24 orten clans; reflexive/middle/emphatic enclitic pronounced [kɛːx] with a final velar fricative and written as a separate word in the Pökoot Bible per Zwarts, Chelimo & Jerono 2024: 539–540); documented in Farler & Wakefield (1882), Johnston (1902), Hon. K. R. Dundas (1910), Beech (1911), Barton (1921), Rottland (1982), and Zwarts, Chelimo & Jerono (2024).

languages.name: Taveta (Kitaveta)
languages.notes: Northeast Coast Bantu (Pare-Taveta group) around Taveta and Lake Jipe; documented in Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894 'Discovery of Lakes Rudolf and Stefanie', Vol. I, Chs. II–IV, pp. 38–208 — audited 100% line-by-line), Steggall (1892–1906), Hollis (1910–1911), Johnston (1919), and BFBS (1921).

languages.name: Daasanach (Dhaasanac)
languages.notes: Lowland East Cushitic (Western Omo-Tana / Galaboid; autonym d’áasannæc, earlier Galab or Geleba) agropastoral and fishing community around Ileret on the northeastern shore of Lake Turkana and Southwest Ethiopia (1994 Ethiopian census: 32,029; 1980 Kenyan est.: 2,500; Tosco est.: 35,000–40,000; shares 53.3% of its 100-word core lexicon with Arbore, 50.0% with Elmolo, 38.9% with Oromo, 35.8% with Konso & Somali, and 35.6% with Rendille); documented in Lieut. Ludwig von Höhnel (1894 as Reshiat, Buma & Marle/Arbore), Gabriele da Trento (1941, 60 units), Eike Haberland (1966, 91 units), Harold C. Fleming (1965, 102 units & 1971, 146 units), M. Lionel Bender (1971, 97 units), Hans-Jürgen Sasse (1973–1984, ca. 11 studies), Mauro Tosco (2001 'The Dhaasanac Language', Kuschitische Sprachstudien Band 17, Köppe, Köln, xiv + 598 pp. + 20 photos, c. 1,400 units), Sumiyo Nishiguchi (2004 'Consonant Assimilation and Sonority : A Case Study in Daasanach', OUPEL Vol. 9, pp. 39–51, OUKA, DOI: 10.18910/70792 — audited 100% line-by-line), and Václav Blažek (2011 'Dasanech Language – State-of-the-Art', Folia Orientalia Vol. 48, Masaryk University, Brno — audited 100% line-by-line).

officialLanguages.role: Language of government, courts, higher education, and media (Article 7(2), Constitution of Kenya 2010)
National lingua franca, parliamentary co-official language, and primary language of inter-ethnic communication (Article 7(1)–(2), Constitution of Kenya 2010)

officialLanguages.language: Kenyan Sign Language (KSL), Braille & Indigenous Languages
officialLanguages.role: Protected and promoted by the State under Article 7(3) of the Constitution of Kenya 2010
